correctness.rationale: For distinct a,b the mixed products cannot collide with either square. If a,b commute, the two product squares coincide exactly when ab⁻¹ has order two, which also detects the quotient collision. If they do not commute and have equal squares, (ab⁻¹)²=1 would imply that ab⁻¹ commutes with b, a contradiction. Thus precisely the noncommuting unequal-square pairs witness size two. If all noncommuting pairs have equal squares, choose one such pair and set c=a²=b². It is central in the generated subgroup. Applying the same condition to (a,ab) and (b,ba) gives (ab)²=(ba)²=c, while (ab)²=c implies ba=ab⁻¹=c⁻¹ab. Squaring forces c=c⁻¹; c=1 would force commutation. The quotient by ⟨c⟩ has two distinct nontrivial commuting involutions represented by a,b and hence order four; the resulting order-eight presentation is quaternion. On {1,a,b} the products are {1,a,b,c,ab,cab} and the quotients are {1,a,ca,b,cb,ab,cab}, establishing size three. For abelian groups, on {0,g,3g} the sum residues 0,1,2,3,4,6 and difference residues 0,±1,±2,±3 give (5,6) at order six and (6,7) at larger orders. Without such an element, primary decomposition gives the listed exceptions or a subgroup C₃², C₅² or C₄×C₂, with direct independent-generator counts (6,7), (6,7), (5,6) on {0,a,b}. Finally, exponent two gives identical sets pointwise and orders three through five saturate both sets whenever 2|A|>|G|; smaller subsets balance by the pair calculation. These arguments cover all quantifiers, including the trivial group and empty subset. The proof in RESULT.md §§1–4 is replayable by exact set arithmetic. evidence: Amit et al. §§1.1–1.2 study proportions and moments; Miller–Vissuet Theorem 1.1 supplies an asymptotic density-one statement.
Penman–Wells classify finite abelian groups with strict sum dominance. Herrmann studies small strict sum-dominant sets. Ascoli et al. and Mandal–Neetu supply family-specific small-size results.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Asymptotically frequent balance permits finite small witnesses. Sum dominance rules out only one sign of discrepancy. Family results cover some cases exactly, not arbitrary groups or the reduction to quaternion subgroups.

evidence: C₆ has no strict sum-dominant set under Penman–Wells, but {0,1,3} has five sums and six differences. Exhaustive three-point counts for dihedral groups restrict the group hypotheses and do not cover the quaternion or general abelian branches.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The inspected general and family-specific statements do not imply the combined universal-exception and minimum-witness result. The calculation for two points and building blocks need not individually be new.

evidence: Mouli–Saldin Theorem 1.1 and Duvivier et al. Theorem 1.5 compare the two quotient sets AA⁻¹ and A⁻¹A.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Replacing AA by the other quotient set is not an equivalent convention: the other condition holds in every abelian group, whereas C₆ already fails the frozen universal equality. Inverting A can switch the right/left quotient framing, but cannot turn AA into the other quotient.

value.rationale: For the standard sum/difference statistic, universal balance is decided by subsets of size at most three, with a sharp size threshold and a local structural obstruction. This is a useful exact complement to larger-subset count and asymptotic-balance results. The quaternion reduction explains why pair testing alone is insufficient even for nonabelian groups; the result is not merely a small-order census.
